doc.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Ellington years, Pearl Bailey and Jazz at the Philharmonic
title: Roommates with Strayhorn and then Duke
summary: Bellson roomed briefly with Strayhorn, then lasted a week with Duke, who wrote through the night while flowers and telegrams arrived.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: I’d like to return again to talking about your experience with Duke Ellington. You mentioned earlier that you were Billy Strayhorn’s roommate. I’m just wondering if you had some experiences to share there? You can tell us what it was like being close to Billy Strayhorn. You mentioned he’s a genius. Of course we all know that.

After that two weeks with Billy Strayhorn, I roomed with Duke. Billy Strayhorn went back home to do some composing or writing. He just came out with the band periodically. But I lasted one week with Duke, because he stays up all night writing music. In the morning when I got up at 9 o’clock, boom, boom, boom, [there’s a] knock on the door – no, 4 o’clock in the morning – [a] knock on the door. “Flowers for Mr. Ellington.” Duke’s busy writing, so I had to answer the doorbell. Flowers, telegram for Mr., flowers, telegram – all night long. I had to answer the door, and I wasn’t getting any sleep. So I finally told Duke – I said, “Duke, if you want a good, strong drummer, I’ve got to get out of here and get some sleep.” He laughed. That was another experience.
Who else did you have for roommates during that two-year stint with Duke? Did you have any other roommates?
After that, I roomed with Tizol a couple of times, and Paul Gonsalves. No, pretty much alone then.
I’m surprised the Duke even had a roommate.
Yeah, right. He laughed when I said, “If you want a good, strong drummer, you better let me get out of here right now.”
